Press Release:


KPMG: The Unravelling
The so-called SARS Rogue Report, compiled by KPMG, had devastating consequences for the
stability of the South African Revenue Services. Then the international auditing firm withdrew its
findings, forcing eight executives and the CEO to resign in the midst of the crisis. But SARS
insists that there’s nothing wrong with the controversial report. Carte Blanche analyses the
damage

Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: For the last three months, the infamous GuptaLeaks documents has drowned the country in revelation, after revelation linked to state capture.

Now, global companies implicated with Gupta entities may be crumbling under the strain of scrutiny with questionable corporate governance exposed on a grand scale.

Some companies like the multi-national auditing firm KPMG are owning up.

LINK: //On Friday last week KPMG made an announcement that was as shocking as it was unexpected. They said they no longer stood by the findings of the so-called rogue unit that had been commissioned by SARS.

VO: This week, a titanic clash between the auditing giant KPMG & the South African Revenue Service was set in motion.

At the centre is, a KPMG report that was commissioned in 2014, by the then newly appointed SARS Commissioner Tom Moyane, at a price tag of R23 million – paid for by taxpayers.

A leaked version of the report found that a covert and rogue intelligence unit was operating unlawfully within SARS.

Professor Ivor Chipkin from the Public Affairs Research Institute believes this was all part of an effort to re-establish control over the South African Revenue Service.

IVOR: SARS was seen to be way to autonomous from political control.

VO: KPMG was to conduct a forensic investigation into an intelligence unit within SARS that investigated high-profile tax offenders. At that stage, there had already been two reports that investigated similar and related allegations.

LINK: The Sikhakhane Commission was an internal process – it was followed by the Kroon report which ratified Sikhakhane’s findings, so the question is why bring in a third organisation in the form of KPMG? When SARS by it’s own admission says its Sikhakhane which has formed the basis of disciplinary proceedings.

VO: Adrian Lackay is a former SARS spokesperson – he was one of the employees that resigned during the wave of rogue unit allegations.

ADRIAN: The KPMG forensic report in my view was always intended to provide some veneer and credibility to the actions SARS had taken or was intending to take.

VO: But that all changed with KPMG’s statement: “Given the failure to appropriately apply our own risk management and quality controls, that part of the report which refers to conclusions, recommendations and legal opinions should no longer be relied upon.”

Advocate Ben Winks has worked in the field of audit regulations – he says it’s an unprecedented move.

BEN: in this case - …. KPMG says that they couldn’t do it…….. legally… as carefully as auditing responsibility require.

LINK: When SARS called it’s press conference – the country was hoping for clarity – instead it got more confusion – instead of focussing on the report’s flaws – SARS chose to focus on procedure and ownership. SARS PRESSER

UPSOUND PRESSER TOM MOYANE
Moyane: This abhorrent, unethical and unprofessional conduct by KPMG has left SARS
with no option but to consider the following legal route: //

VO: Commissioner Moyane outlined legal action for reputational damage, reporting KPMG to statutory bodies, to the Finance Minister and Parliament for investigation. While making it clear that the report was the “exclusive property of SARS”.

We spoke to SARS representative Luther Lebelo.

LUTHER: We have no reason to doubt the report, because no body has shown where to doubt the report. You understand the logic
JOHN: actually I don’t, they authors are saying they longer stand by it..
LUTHER: we have no reason to doubt it. Not given a reason.
JOHN: Some reason is a reason
LUTHER: not enough of a reason – let’s leave it there. You understand.

IVOR: They have to stand by that report – the actions in SARS have been legitimised by report – if not questions leadership own legitimacy.

JOHN: if KPMG says they made a mistake why is your issue around ownership, service level agreement, why does it not concern the truth?
LUTHER: What is the purpose of the law. This is constitutional democracy my brother – there is a constitution that protects people’s rights – its the SARS rights – the right not to be KPMG abuse their rights.

VO: According to SARS, it’s a copyright and intellectual property matter – but it doesn’t apply in this case says Advocate Winks.

BEN: KPMG can not contract out of its statutory obligations to the South African public – that is to a registered auditor it’s highest duty ethically and legally.

VO: Eight KPMG South Africa Executives, including CEO, Trever Hoole, resigned last week.

IVOR: There’s been an admission in practice if not in words that they’ve been involved in some pretty awful stuff.

LINK: KPMG is less about cooking the books, than it is about manipulating the facts that in part contributed to driving South Africa into political and economic crisis.

VO: KPMG’s CEO Nhlamu Dlomu is the new face of the embattled firm – she appeared on Talk Radio 702.

BRUCE WHITFIELD INTERVIEW UPSOUND:
KPMG CEO: we have been engaging with everyone now – and we are inviting commentary from our fiercest critics even - we want to engage and hear what the concerns are, so that we can react on time.

VO: The company will pay back the R23 million SARS fee, and an additional R40 million they claim to have earned from Gupta companies.

Former Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan – says it’s far from adequate.

Contrary to the report, KPMG now states the evidence in the documentation provided doesn’t support the interpretation that Gordhan knew or ought to have known about the rogue nature of the unit.

But other than that, some say the firm’s statement is vague about what exactly KPMG no longer stands by.

ADRIAN: KPMG found they were very explicit in their findings that a covert rogue intelligence unit existed that broke the law, that spied on tax payers, that obtained information illegally – if you want to apologise then withdraw those findings as explicitly as you made them.

VO: On Thursday night, a KPMG International delegation met with Gordhan and his former deputy Mcebisi Jonas who maintain that the firm has a moral duty to account for their conduct.

In the meantime, KPMG is starting to feel the heat – with two big corporate clients, Sasfin & Hulisani dropping the auditors and Business Leadership SA suspending their membership.

The SARS report revelation also cast the spotlight on KPMG’s independence

ADRIAN: They didn’t always make their own findings. Now, KPMG describes there report as an independent forensic report – where’s the independence there?

JOHN: Because KPMG were instructed, by your own lawyers what findings and recommendation to make and those were copy & paste – it’s in the documents
LUTHER: Who told that you that?
JOHN: … or we can deal with the issue…

VO: Luther tried to spin his way out of this one. But what is clear, is how blatantly some of the parts were copied & pasted.

The document on the left is the memo from the SARS law firm. Parts of it appear word for word on the right in KPMG’s Executive Findings & Conclusions.

BEN: An auditor needs to disclose the fact that they sought the advice from an expert and still express opinion independently from that.

VO: Nowhere in the leaked version does KPMG make reference to it being the opinion of the law firm – it was presented as their own – something it seems they owned up to in their statement:

“KPMG South Africa acknowledges that such opinions should have been caveated as recommendations of legal advisors and not formulated in the manner contained in the report.”

LINK: So in the end what we’re left with is three reports the credibility of which has been questioned in varying degrees – it’s a characteristic of this entire saga that there never seems to be simple answer to a simple question.

JOHN: it surprises me that you can say such sweeping things around conspiracy – KPMG own’s demise.
LUTHER: concerted effort – moyane not competent – media part of that and other elements who are part of that.

VO: But without the facts, it’s just an opinion.

ADRIAN: That public institution must ultimately be accountable to South Africans, it is funded with public money – and people have every right to ask serious questions when they have serious doubts about the conduct of SARS.

VO: But if anything has come out this week’s saga – it’s a strong message to corporates who stand accused of selling out the country – civil society is watching.

IVOR: They will be found out and there will be severe consequences for them.


 
PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: A titanic clash looms between KPMG & SARS as the embattled auditing firm struggles to survival amidst threats of legal action and boycotts.

PROMO 2
VO: As KPMG said parts of the so-called Rogue Unit Report should no longer be relied upon, SARS chose to stand by the report.

LUTHER: We have no reason to doubt the report, because no body has shown where to doubt the report.

PROMO 3
VO: In the wake of the GuptaLeaks – 8 KMPG executives resign and the company apoligises to the country for their failings.

IVOR: There’s been an admission in practice if not in words that they’ve been involved in some pretty awful stuff. M14
